## Source

I extended Patricio Romero's [Exploring Vehicle Fuel Efficiency with Tidyverse](https://github.com/DW8888/fall2027-data607-tidyverse-assignment/blob/main/vehicle_fuel_efficiency_tidyverse.qmd) vignette. His work uses `dplyr` and `ggplot2` to compare fuel efficiency by vehicle class.

My extension adds `tidyr::pivot_longer()`. I use it to place city and highway MPG in the same column, then compare both values in one table and chart.

## Load the data

```{r}
# tidyverse includes dplyr, tidyr, and ggplot2.
# knitr is used to display the summary table.
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

# The mpg dataset is included with ggplot2, so no separate CSV is needed.
data("mpg", package = "ggplot2")
```

## Change the table from wide to long

The original data stores city MPG in `cty` and highway MPG in `hwy`. I used `pivot_longer()` so both measurements use one `road_type` column and one `mpg` column.

```{r}
# Keep the vehicle class and the two MPG columns.
# Rename cty and hwy so the labels are easier to understand.
mpg_long <- mpg |>
  select(class, city = cty, highway = hwy) |>
  # Stack city and highway into one road-type column.
  pivot_longer(
    cols = c(city, highway),
    names_to = "road_type",
    values_to = "mpg"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    class = recode(
      class,
      "2seater" = "Two Seater",
      "compact" = "Compact",
      "midsize" = "Mid-Size",
      "minivan" = "Minivan",
      "pickup" = "Pickup",
      "subcompact" = "Subcompact",
      "suv" = "SUV"
    ),
    road_type = str_to_title(road_type)
  )

mpg_long |>
  slice_head(n = 8) |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Vehicle class", "Road type", "MPG"),
    caption = "City and highway MPG in a longer table"
  )
```

The row count changes from 234 to 468 because every vehicle now has one city row and one highway row. No vehicle was added or removed.

## Calculate the averages

```{r}
# Calculate one average for each vehicle class and road type.
mpg_summary <- mpg_long |>
  group_by(class, road_type) |>
  summarise(
    vehicles = n(),
    average_mpg = round(mean(mpg), 1),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(class, road_type)

mpg_summary |>
  kable(
    col.names = c("Vehicle class", "Road type", "Vehicles", "Average MPG"),
    caption = "Average city and highway MPG by vehicle class"
  )
```

The table shows that every class has a higher highway average than city average. Compact and subcompact vehicles have the highest highway averages in this dataset.

## Compare both road types in one chart

```{r}
#| label: fig-city-highway-extension
#| fig-alt: "Grouped bar chart comparing average city and highway miles per gallon for seven vehicle classes. Highway MPG is higher for every class."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5
# The two road types use charcoal and orange, with printed values for accessibility.
# The value labels also show the difference without depending only on color.
ggplot(
  mpg_summary,
  aes(
    x = class,
    y = average_mpg,
    fill = road_type
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    width = 0.68,
    color = "#333333"
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(label = average_mpg),
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.75),
    hjust = -0.15,
    size = 3.2
  ) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("City" = "#666666", "Highway" = "#E69F00")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(
    title = "Average city and highway MPG by vehicle class",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Average miles per gallon",
    fill = "Road type"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
```

## Summary

My extension adds a new Tidyverse step to the original work. `pivot_longer()` makes it possible to group city and highway values under one variable. This makes the comparison easier to summarize and graph without writing separate code for each road type.
